title: What to eat
intro: Izumo soba (stacked in lacquered warigo trays, eaten with all three tiers at once) and Lake Shinji's shijimi-clam cuisine are the two dishes this trip is actually built around — both are specific to Shimane, not generic "Japanese food."

items.name: Tanakaya
items.hours: 11:00–16:00 or until the soba sells out
items.why: Three-color warigo soba, a 5-minute walk from the shrine, open on the Wednesday this trip visits (unlike the more famous Arakiya).
items.crowd_tip: Forms a line at midday — arrive right at 11:00 or plan for a wait.

items.name: Arakiya
items.hours: 11:00–16:00 or until the soba sells out
items.closed: Wednesdays (and the following day if Wednesday is a public holiday)
items.why: Izumo's oldest soba house, trading since the 1780s — worth it on any day but Wednesday.

items.name: Yakumoan
items.how: Renovated samurai residence near the castle moat
items.closed: Jan 1–2; no weekly closure day confirmed on the operator's own page
items.why: Soba in a converted samurai house, and the party-size test for this trip: the official page doesn't list a group cap, so call ahead (0852-22-2400) to confirm seating for 8 before walking over.

items.name: Matsu-no-Daidokoro Konekkoya
items.why: Shinjiko-shichin (the lake's 7 signature foods — shijimi clams, whitebait, eel) in a 24-seat banquet hall built for groups — comfortably fits the full party of 8. No private-room buyout, so expect other diners nearby. Sister restaurant Nekkoya (Isemiya-cho, same operator) has an exact-fit fully private 8-seat room if the group wants total separation instead, though its menu is general Shimane izakaya fare rather than this lake-view shichimi theme.

items.name: Gungendo Main Store Café
items.how: In the Omori townscape, on the walking route to the mine
items.why: A 170-year-old renovated merchant house with a courtyard garden — the obvious indoor/lunch stop on the Iwami Ginzan day (open Thursdays, when this trip visits).
